scenario: AITA for playing music in the middle of the day when my roommate has a weird sleep schedule? | So I live in a 3 bedroom duplex with 2 other girls. The duplex is laid out with two bedrooms up stairs with a bathroom in the middle. Downstairs is the living room, kitchen, dining room and roomates room and her own bathroom. When we picked rooms I picked first because I moved in first and then my roommate upstairs picked and then the girl downstairs. She wasn’t too happy with her room because it was the smallest and the location but settled because she had her own bathroom. So the roommate downstairs has a very weird schedule. Sometimes she works nights and sometimes mornings. Sometimes she has 5 hour days and other days she can work 13. So obviously with the constant changing work schedule her sleeping schedule has became very weird and erratic and we never know when she’s asleep now. So since I can never guess when she’s asleep I often so downstairs in the kitchen and make food and play music on my speaker while I meal prep. It’s apart of my routine through out the day that i really enjoy since I don’t work till 2pm. But yesterday my roommate downstairs texted our group chat and asked us to please stop playing music in the kitchen at any time of the day. She said it wakes her up almost every time and when she is a wake it’s just very disruptive. My other roommate said sure but I said that’s not really fair because she often plays music too in the kitchen. She told me it wasn’t really fair that she had the shittiest room in the house and that if I wanted to switch with her so she wouldn’t have to be woken up by it that would be fine. Of course I said no and said I was going to keep playing music because it’s noon usually when I do it and it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule. Both my roommates are saying I’m being an asshole and that it’s the least I can do because I have the best room in the house because it’s the most separate. I honestly think they are being assholes because why should I have to be so quiet I’m the middle of the day!?

AITA for playing music in the middle of the day when my roommate has a weird sleep schedule? | So I live in a 3 bedroom duplex with 2 other girls. When we picked rooms I picked first because I moved in first and then my roommate upstairs picked and then the girl downstairs. It’s apart of my routine through out the day that i really enjoy since I don’t work till 2pm. But yesterday my roommate downstairs texted our group chat and asked us to please stop playing music in the kitchen at any time of the day. Of course I said no and said I was going to keep playing music because it’s noon usually when I do it and it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule. Both my roommates are saying I’m being an asshole and that it’s the least I can do because I have the best room in the house because it’s the most separate. I honestly think they are being assholes because why should I have to be so quiet I’m the middle of the day!?

prediction.raw: I’d give this scenario a **0/1**—meaning it’s a **borderline case** where both perspectives have valid points, but the outcome depends on **balance, communication, and compromise**. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Not Just "Wrong" (1 Point for Fairness):** 1. **Your Routine is Legitimate** – Music during meal prep is a personal preference that many people enjoy, and it’s not inherently disruptive *if* it’s reasonable (e.g., not blasting headphones at 3 AM). Your roommate’s issue isn’t that you play music—it’s that *her* sleep schedule is incompatible with it, and she has no control over when you do it. 2. **You’re Not the Only One Who Uses the Kitchen** – Your roommate *does* play music too, so there’s inconsistency in the rules. If she’s okay with her own noise, why should you be penalized for hers? 3. **Your Room is "Better"** – You’re right that your room is more private (upstairs), but that doesn’t automatically mean you get to impose your habits on shared spaces. The kitchen is a communal area, and its use should accommodate *all* residents, not just the one who’s least affected by noise. --- ### **Why It’s Not Just "Right" (0 Points for Assholery):** 1. **Her Sleep Schedule is a Real Issue** – Even if her work hours are unpredictable, *she* is the one directly affected by your music. If she’s asking for a simple adjustment (lower volume, different times, or a headphone rule), that’s a reasonable request—not an unreasonable demand. 2. **You’re Ignoring the Power Dynamic** – You moved in first, so you *did* have first pick of rooms, but that doesn’t mean you get to dictate the rules of shared living. Your roommate’s room *is* the smallest and least ideal, but that doesn’t negate her right to a peaceful living environment. 3. **No Compromise Attempted** – You dismissed her request outright ("it’s noon, it’s ridiculous") without even considering alternatives: - **Lower volume** (e.g., no speaker, just headphones). - **Specific times** (e.g., no music before 10 AM or after 6 PM). - **A shared "quiet hours" rule** (even if not strict, a general understanding). - **Switching rooms** (if she’s *that* bothered, but this seems like a last resort). 4. **Your Roommate’s Frustration is Valid** – She’s not just annoyed—she’s *disrupted* in her sleep, which affects her well-being. If you were in her shoes, would you be okay with someone playing music in the kitchen every time they’re awake, regardless of your schedule? --- ### **The Real Issue: Shared Living = Shared Responsibility** This isn’t about "fairness" in a zero-sum way—it’s about **mutual respect**. You can’t expect to live with others without considering how your habits affect them, even if you feel like your routine is harmless to you. **What You Could Have Done Instead:** - **Acknowledge her concern** ("I hear you, I’ll try to keep it quieter"). - **Propose a compromise** (e.g., "I’ll turn it down if you’re sleeping"). - **Set a rule together** (e.g., "No speaker music in the kitchen after 10 AM"). **What You Should Do Now:** - **Apologize** (not just "sorry you’re mad," but "I realize I didn’t think about how this affects you"). - **Adjust your habits** (even if it’s just lowering the volume). - **Reaffirm shared living standards** (e.g., "Let’s all agree on kitchen noise rules"). --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (But Fix It)** You’re not *wrong* for enjoying music, but you’re **wrong for dismissing her needs without compromise**. Roommateship requires give-and-take, and right now, you’re coming across as selfish rather than just stubborn. **Fix it before it escalates.** *(And if she’s still unhappy after you adjust, then maybe the room swap conversation is worth revisiting—but not as a threat, as a solution.)*
